en: The Sūtra on the Eightfold Noble Path, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Buddha...
He addressed his disciples:
"Listen as I speak of the wrong path and also the right path.
What is the wrong path?"

Not seeing with clarity, not reflecting with clarity, not speaking with clarity, not governing with clarity, not seeking with clarity, not acting with clarity, not intending with clarity, and not concentrating with clarity.
These are the eight wrong practices of the path.
What are the eight right practices of the path?
The first is right view.
What is meant by "seeing with clarity"?

It is to have faith in giving, faith in ritual, faith in sacrifice, faith that good and evil deeds naturally bring merit, faith in one's parents, faith in the world’s practitioners of the Way, faith in the pursuit of the Way, faith in clear conduct, and faith in clear reception.
"In this world and the next, one who is wise attains realization and achieves it for oneself.
One then informs others, saying, 'This is the vision of truth.
What is the second truth of mindfulness? "
To renounce desires of the mind, renounce the household life, to be without anger or resentment, and not to harm one another—this is called right mindfulness.
What is the third, right speech?
Not to engage in double-tongued speech, not to repeat words [to one person for the purpose of causing discord], not to utter abusive language, and not to speak falsehoods—this is truthful speech.
"What is the fourth truth of conduct?
Abstaining from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—this is called the practice of truth.
What is the fifth, the acceptance of truth?

It is when a disciple of the Way seeks the Dharma through hearing; he must not seek it through what is not the Dharma. He seeks food, bedding, and medicine for illness through the True Dharma; he must not seek them through what is not the Dharma. This is called the acceptance of truth.
"What is the remedy for the sixth truth?

It is the practice of the mind in conjunction with the cycle of birth and death; it is the practice of diligent application, the practice of exerting effort through causes and conditions, and the maintenance of the mind through diligence without weariness—this is the remedy for the truth."
"What is the seventh, the truth of intention (*saṃkalpa-satya*)?
It is the unerring and non-common seeking of intention that accords with and inclines toward the mental engagement with the formations of birth and death; this is called the truth of intention."
"What is the eighth truth of concentration?
It is the union of the mind with the cycle of birth and death, wherein mindfulness ceases, signs cease, guarding ceases, and the aggregates cease.
One does not act, one commits no transgression, and one does not fall into the intermediate state."
This is called the certainty of the truths.
"Monks! All disciples of the Way should receive these eightfold practices of the path of truth; by practicing as taught, they may attain the realization of the eightfold path."

Those who see clearly believe in giving, for they know that in future lives one will obtain full merit; those who believe in worship see that offering salutations to śramaṇas and practitioners brings merit; those who believe in sacrifice hang silk banners, burn incense, scatter flowers, and light lamps; those who believe in the practice of the ten wholesome paths know that this naturally results in the attainment of merit; those who believe in their parents believe in filial piety and obedience; those who believe in the world’s practitioners joyfully receive the sutras; and those who believe in the seekers of the Way dedicate themselves to practicing the Way.
The practitioner who has faith in the truths abandons evil intent; the recipient who has faith in the truths does not violate the precepts.
In this life and the next, being wise oneself leads to the attainment of wisdom; one who is able to teach others to attain realization becomes a true person through self-perfection.
To be able to bring others to fulfillment and then communicate this to them is called "seeing and knowing the truth.
In this way, one liberates oneself and liberates others. Regarding the second truth:

that which arises from the mind is the loss of the mind; for one who wishes to leave the household life, it is the mindfulness of the Path; for one who is not prone to anger or resentment, it is patience; and for one who does not encroach upon others, it is right intention.
"Third, truthful speech means not reviling others and not committing the four verbal transgressions, but speaking only of the essential truths of the path-factors with utmost sincerity.
Fourth, truthful conduct means refraining from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, and practicing sincerity and trustworthiness."
"The fifth truth is that one who does not fall into greed merely seeks one robe and one meal as a lowly physician.
The sixth truth is that the practitioner turns toward the Sūtra of the Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment."
"The seventh truth, *mānasa* (mind), is the daily increase of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharma*), never departing from the mind.

"The eighth truth, *śamatha* (calm abiding), is not forgetting dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). As for 'abiding,' it is the constant returning of the mind to its protection; as for 'having already abided,' it is being free from all transgressions; as for 'gathering in abiding,' it is attaining the path of merit."
Thus spoke the Buddha.
They all received it with joy.
The Sūtra on the Eightfold Noble Path Spoken by the Buddha.
